usage_notes.narrative: Laukens places maj7 chords in the tonic-major family, the resolution target of ii-V-I progressions in major keys (chapter 3 p. 13; chapter 6 p. 200).
Paradigm minor-triad-over-major: 'You can play a minor triad starting on the 3rd of a major chord. For example: Em over Cmaj7' (chapter 8 p. 289).
'Pattern 72 features an Am7 arpeggio over Cmaj7 and can also be used over Am7' (chapter 7 p. 253) — relative-minor arpeggio produces maj9 colour without root-position shape.
'Major bebop scale = major scale + b6' as the idiomatic scale over maj7 chords; guitar requires slides for chromatic passing tone (chapter 7 p. 243).
Characteristic colour move: chromatic descending line between the 7 and 5 of the major chord (chapter 8 p. 285).
'Pattern 57 starts with a G6 arpeggio and can be used on major or dominant chords' (chapter 6 p. 200).
'Pattern 47 is an extension of pattern 43, but this one can only be used on major chords because it contains the 7th' (chapter 5 p. 150).
min7 chords as ii in major ii-V-I and iv in minor (chapter 4 p. 100; chapter 7 p. 240). Dm7 is the paradigm ii chord throughout Studies 4-8.
Wes Montgomery prescription: 'You can play a major triad or maj7 chord on the third of a major chord. For example: Fmaj7 (or F) over Dm7' (chapter 4 p. 100; chapter 8 p. 280).
'You can play a minor triad starting on the 5th of a minor chord. For example: Am over Dm7' (chapter 8 p. 289).

'Augmented chords are often used to play over minor chords, resulting in a minor/major 7 sound. Over a minor chord you can play an augmented triad or maj7#5 arpeggio, both built on the b3' (chapter 4 p. 100; chapter 7 p. 251).
'Minor bebop scale = Dorian mode + 7' as idiomatic scale over min7; guitar uses slides for chromatic passing tone (chapter 7 p. 242).
'The G dominant bebop scale can be played over: G7, G9, G13; Gsus4; Dm7 (in a II VI in C major)' (chapter 7 p. 240) — covers ii-V pair simultaneously.
'Pattern 42 circles around the b3 of Dm7 and contains a minor 1235 pattern starting on the second note' (chapter 5 p. 150) — circling of b3 distinguishes from major-context counterpart.
'if you play an Am triad over Dm7, you can lower one fret and play Abm over G7' (chapter 8 p. 290) — fingerboard shortcut connecting ii-V triad substitutions.
V chord in both major and minor ii-V-I and the most heavily substituted chord quality in the method (chapter 3 p. 13).
'Playing a half-diminished arpeggio from the 3rd of a dominant chord brings out the 9 sound. For example: Bm7b5 over G7' (chapter 3 p. 13; chapter 6 p. 200) — 'very common substitution.'

'Playing Dm over G7 is a technique Wes Montgomery would often use in his solos' (chapter 3 p. 13). Systematic formulation: 'You can play a minor triad starting on the 5th of a dominant chord. For example: Dm over G7' (chapter 8 p. 290).
'The dominant bebop scale is a Mixolydian mode with a descending chromatic note between the root and the b7' (chapter 7 p. 240-241). Primary scale resource over G7, G9, G13.

'You can play the tonic harmonic minor scale over any dominant chord. For example: C harmonic minor over G7... creates a 7b9, b13 sound... Another name for the harmonic minor scale played over a dominant chord is the Phrygian dominant scale' (chapter 5 p. 150).
'Pattern 82 uses tritone substitution by playing a Bb7 arpeggio over E7' (chapter 8 p. 287) — tritone-sub dominant generates full altered sound via chromatic voice-leading.
'Dominants going to major chords can use the regular 1235 pattern. Dominants going to minor chords require a b9 instead of a 9' (chapter 4 p. 100).
'An augmented 7th arpeggio or triad is a convenient way to bring out an altered sound on dominant chords' (chapter 3 p. 13).

'Pattern 83 starts with the chromatic part of the G (dominant) bebop scale and continues with a G7 arpeggio' (chapter 8 p. 288) — standard bebop construction of chromatic approach leading to arpeggio.
'Pattern 86 combines an Em7 arpeggio with a chromatic line' (chapter 8 p. 293) — Em7 = upper-structure minor 7th from 6th/13th over G7.

'You can also play this pattern over dominant chords by changing the natural 7 to a b7 (the 5th note in the pattern)' (chapter 8 p. 286) — one-pitch change separates maj7 from dom7 pattern application.
Ab minor triad over G7: 'The triad brings out a sus4 sound (C) with the altered tensions b9 (Ab) and b13 (Eb)' (chapter 3 p. 13).
'This last pattern voice leads from 13 to b13 to the 9 of C major' (chapter 8 p. 294) — chromatic descending motion through 13th smooths dominant-to-tonic resolution.
'Notice the voice leading going from the 5th of Dm7, to the b9 of G7, to the 5th of Cmaj7. This is a common voice leading over a II V I' (chapter 7 p. 246).

dom7b9 within altered-dominant family, produced when harmonic minor (Phrygian dominant) played over V7 in minor ii-V-I; 7b9/b13 sound is defining colour of V7 in minor contexts (chapter 3 p. 13; chapter 5 p. 150).

'Diminished arpeggios are a common way to play over dominant chord and produce a 7b9 sound. Playing a diminished arpeggio from the b9, 3, 5, or b7 of a dominant chord brings out the b9 sound. For example: Abdim7 over G7' (chapter 5 p. 150).
'Here, I switch from a Bm7b5 arpeggio to a Bdim7 arpeggio, going from the 9 to the b9' (chapter 6 p. 200) — half-diminished to diminished switch intensifies dominant tension.
'Dominants going to minor chords require a b9 instead of a 9' (chapter 4 p. 100) — single alteration converts major-resolving dominant line into minor-resolving one.
dom7alt = maximally tense V chord with all four altered tones (b9, #9, b5/b13) from altered scale (7th mode of melodic minor); G altered scale = Ab melodic minor from G (chapter 6 p. 200).

'The altered scale contains all four of the common altered notes (b9-#9-b5-b13), which are used to create tension over the underlying chord' (chapter 6 p. 200). Used over dom7 in both major and minor keys.
'One of the arpeggios contained in the altered scale is the Gaug7' (chapter 6 p. 200) — discrete melodic unit extracted rather than running scale stepwise.
'Another useful arpeggio in the altered scale is the Bmaj7#5' (chapter 6 p. 200) — higher-register altered color distinct from Gaug7.
'Another useful arpeggio in the altered scale is the Abm/maj7' (chapter 6 p. 200) — completes the three-arpeggio systematic altered-scale extraction set.
'You can play an m(add9) over altered dominant chords, starting on the b9. For example: Fm(add9) over E7#9' (chapter 4 p. 100) — produces #9 and b13 colors.
'You can play a minor triad starting on the b9 of a dominant chord. For example: Abm over G7' (chapter 8 p. 290) — most altered of minor-triad-over-dominant substitutions.
'This is a typical altered scale run starting on the b13' (chapter 8 p. 281) — b13 immediately projects altered color before descent through remaining tensions.
min7b5 as ii in minor ii-V-I, paired with V7alt or V7b9, resolving to minor tonic. Bm7b5-E7alt-Am is the paradigm (chapter 3 p. 13).
'You can play a maj7 chord over a half-diminished chord, starting on the b5 of that half-diminished chord. For example: Fmaj7 over Bm7b5' (chapter 3 p. 13) — produces #11 color.
'You can play a m(add9) arpeggio over half-diminished chords, starting on the b3. For example: Dm(add9) over Bm7b5' (chapter 4 p. 100).
'The G dominant bebop scale can be played over: ... Bm7b5 (in a II VI in A minor)' (chapter 7 p. 240) — bridges half-dim ii and dominant V in minor ii-V.
'This Cmaj7 arpeggio can be used over Cmaj7, Am7, or F#m7b5' (chapter 5 p. 150) — single arpeggio shape serves three harmonic targets simultaneously.
Within the dominant substitution family — not as independent chords but as arpeggio shapes deployed over dominants to produce b9 coloration (chapter 5 p. 150; chapter 6 p. 200).

'The convenient thing about diminished chords and arpeggios is that their inversions are identical in shape and notes' due to stacked minor thirds — every inversion of Cdim7 uses same fingering (chapter 5 p. 150).

'Playing a diminished arpeggio from the b9, 3, 5, or b7 of a dominant chord brings out the b9 sound. For example: Abdim7 over G7' (chapter 5 p. 150) — all four entry points yield same shape due to symmetry.
Sus4 within dominant family: 'The G dominant bebop scale can be played over: G7, G9, G13; Gsus4; Dm7' (chapter 7 p. 240) — sus4 as dominant color variant, not independent quality.
Ab minor triad over G7 — 'The triad brings out a sus4 sound (C) with the altered tensions b9 (Ab) and b13 (Eb)' (chapter 3 p. 13) — sus4 reachable via b9-rooted minor triad sub.
'One of the arpeggios contained in the altered scale is the Gaug7' (chapter 6 p. 200) — aug7 as superimposition shape over dom7alt, not independent quality.
'its inversions look exactly the same, so you can just slide the same shape 4 frets up or down and essentially get the same chord' (chapter 4 p. 100) — mirrors dim7 symmetry rule.

'Augmented triads can also be used to solo over dominant #11 chords... For example: Db7#11 going to Cmaj7. Because Db7#11 is a substitution for G7alt, you can use a G augmented triad over that chord' (chapter 4 p. 100).
